## Overview

Native screens form a stack, exactly like a native iOS `UINavigationController` or an Android Activity stack. From
inside a `NativeComponent`, you push, pop, and replace screens using methods on `$this`.

## Registering routes

Native routes are registered similarly to Livewire routes, but instead of using `Route::livewire()` you use the
`Route::native()` macro:

```php
use App\NativeComponents\Home;
use App\NativeComponents\ItemDetail;

Route::native('/', Home::class);
Route::native('/item/{id}', ItemDetail::class);
```

You can put these routes anywhere that makes sense for your application, but you may find that creating a
`routes/mobile.php` to keep them all together is a clean option.

Route parameters work just like Laravel web routes — `{id}` matches a path segment and is exposed to the screen
through `$this->param('id')`.

See [Layouts](layouts) for how to attach shared chrome to a route or group of routes, and
[Middleware](middleware) for guarding screens with `->middleware()`.

## Pushing a new screen

```php
$this->navigate('/item/42');
```

By default a push slides in from the right. Pass arbitrary data along with the navigation:

```php
$this->navigate('/item/42', ['source' => 'home-feed']);
```

The next screen reads the data with `$this->data('source')`.

## Going back

```php
$this->back();
```

Pops the current screen off the stack and returns to whatever was beneath it. The default transition is a slide-out
to the right.

## Replacing the current screen

```php
$this->replace('/login');
```

Pops the current screen and pushes a new one in its place — useful after sign-in / sign-out or for in-place tab
swaps. The default transition is a fade.

<aside>

`<native:bottom-nav-item>` taps automatically use `replace` semantics, so the back chevron pops the entire tabs
section in one step rather than stepping through tab history.

</aside>

## Exiting to the web view

```php
$this->exitToWeb('/dashboard');
```

Tear down the native UI stack and load the given URL in the web view. Use this for screens that aren't part of the
native experience.

## Custom transitions

Chain `transition()` after a navigation method to override the default animation:

```php
use Native\Mobile\Edge\Transition;

$this->navigate('/item/42')->transition(Transition::SlideFromBottom);
```

Available cases:

- `Transition::SlideFromRight` - default for `navigate()`
- `Transition::SlideFromLeft` - default for `back()`
- `Transition::SlideFromBottom` - modal-style presentation
- `Transition::Fade` - default for `replace()`
- `Transition::FadeFromBottom` - subtle vertical fade
- `Transition::ScaleFromCenter` - zoom-in effect
- `Transition::ParallaxPush` - incoming screen slides in from the right while the outgoing screen drifts partially left underneath
- `Transition::Morph` <x-docs.version-badge since="4.7" /> - cross-fade while elements that share a `ref` move between the two screens. See [Morphing elements between screens](#morphing-elements-between-screens)
- `Transition::None` - swap with no animation

## Navigating from Blade

The `@navigate` directive triggers navigation directly from your view, with no component method required. It works on
any node, so any element can become a navigation target.

The short form takes a route in single quotes:

@verbatim
```blade
<native:pressable @navigate='/item/42' class="w-full p-4">
    <native:text>View item</native:text>
</native:pressable>
```
@endverbatim

To pass data along with the navigation, use the args form — a route followed by an array:

@verbatim
```blade
<native:pressable @navigate="'/item/42', ['source' => 'home-feed']">
    <native:text>View item</native:text>
</native:pressable>
```
@endverbatim

The next screen reads the data with `$this->data('source')`, exactly as with `$this->navigate()`.

Double quotes hold a PHP expression rather than a plain route, so `@navigate="/item/42"` won't compile. For a
dynamic route, build the string in PHP: `@navigate="'/item/' . $item->id"`.

### Transition modifiers

Add a transition as a modifier to override the default push animation:

@verbatim
```blade
<native:pressable @navigate.slideFromBottom='/item/42'>
    <native:text>Present modally</native:text>
</native:pressable>
```
@endverbatim

Available transition modifiers:

- `fade`
- `slideFromRight`
- `slideFromLeft`
- `slideFromBottom`
- `fadeFromBottom`
- `scaleFromCenter`
- `parallaxPush`
- `morph` <x-docs.version-badge since="4.7" />
- `none`

### Action modifiers

Modifiers also select the navigation action. Use these in place of a route to `back`, or combine them with a route
to `replace` or `exitToWeb`:

@verbatim
```blade
<native:pressable @navigate.back>
    <native:text>Go back</native:text>
</native:pressable>

<native:pressable @navigate.replace='/login'>
    <native:text>Sign out</native:text>
</native:pressable>

<native:pressable @navigate.exitToWeb='/dashboard'>
    <native:text>Open dashboard</native:text>
</native:pressable>
```
@endverbatim

Transition and action modifiers can be combined — `@navigate.replace.fade='/login'`.

## Morphing elements between screens

<x-docs.version-badge since="4.7" />

The morph transition carries an element from where it sits on one screen to where it sits on the next. A thumbnail
grows into a header image, or an avatar slides into place on a profile page. If you've used the web's View
Transitions API, it's the same idea.

Give the element the same `ref` on both screens, then navigate with the `morph` modifier:

@verbatim
```blade
{{-- The album list --}}
@foreach ($albums as $album)
    <native:pressable @navigate.morph="'/album/' . $album->id">
        <native:image :ref="'album-' . $album->id" :src="$album->cover" class="w-16 h-16 rounded-xl" />
    </native:pressable>
@endforeach
```
@endverbatim

@verbatim
```blade
{{-- The album screen --}}
<native:column class="w-full">
    <native:image :ref="'album-' . $album->id" :src="$album->cover" class="w-full h-80" />

    <native:pressable @navigate.back.morph>
        <native:text>Back</native:text>
    </native:pressable>
</native:column>
```
@endverbatim

Tapping an album cross-fades the two screens while the cover moves and grows from the small tile into the header.
Going back with `@navigate.back.morph` plays it in reverse.

From a component, pass `Transition::Morph`:

```php
use Native\Mobile\Edge\Transition;

$this->navigate('/album/3')->transition(Transition::Morph);
```

### Shaping the morph

These attributes change how an element travels. They're read from the element on the screen you're navigating to,
so put them on both elements if you want the same motion in both directions.

- `morph` - what moves. `frame` (the default) moves and resizes the element. `position` moves it at its final size.
  `size` resizes it in place, at its final position. `none` stops the element morphing.
- `morph-duration` - length in milliseconds. The default is `350`, the same as the cross-fade behind it.
- `morph-easing` - the curve: `linear`, `ease-in`, `ease-out`, `ease-in-out` (the default) or `spring`.

@verbatim
```blade
<native:column ref="now-playing" morph="position" morph-duration="500" morph-easing="spring">
    ...
</native:column>
```
@endverbatim

<aside>

On Android, `position` and `size` behave like `frame`. Compose's shared element API always animates the whole frame,
so the element moves and resizes together.

</aside>

### Which elements morph

- An element morphs only when its `ref` is on both screens. Everything else cross-fades with its screen.
- Elements only morph under the `morph` transition. A `ref` that appears on both screens does nothing during a slide
  or a fade.
- Keep each `ref` unique within a screen. If two elements share one, you can't be sure which of them moves.
- `ref` is also how [tests target elements](../testing/interactions#by-ref). If you've reused a test `ref` on two
  screens and don't want those elements to morph, add `morph="none"` to either of them.

### Native chrome

A morph needs one whole screen to replace another. Inside native chrome that doesn't always happen. Pushing from one
screen with a native top bar to another, or switching between tabs of a bottom nav, is animated by the platform's
own navigation, and nothing morphs.

Morphs do run between screens that have no native chrome, and whenever the chrome changes, such as a tab screen
opening a detail screen that has a top bar instead. See [Layouts](layouts) for how screens get their chrome.

## Reading params and data

```php
class ItemDetail extends NativeComponent
{
    public function mount(): void
    {
        $id = $this->param('id');                  // from the route URI
        $source = $this->data('source', 'unknown'); // from navigate()'s second arg

        // ...
    }
}
```

Both accessors take an optional default that's returned when the key is missing.

## Resolving named routes

If you've named your routes you can use `route()` on the component to resolve them to URIs:

```php
$this->navigate($this->route('listing.show', ['id' => 5]));
```

This delegates to Laravel's URL generator with `absolute: false`.

## Customizing device-back behavior

By default, the device back button (Android) pops the navigation stack. Override `onBackPressed()` to add custom
behavior:

```php
class CheckoutForm extends NativeComponent
{
    public bool $dirty = false;

    public function onBackPressed(): void
    {
        if ($this->dirty) {
            $this->showDiscardConfirmation();

            return;
        }

        $this->back();
    }
}
```

If the back press should ultimately still pop, call `$this->back()` from your override.

title: Layouts
order: 154
---

## Overview

Layouts are **optional**. They're the tool for chrome that's shared across *many* screens — a top nav bar, a bottom
tab bar, or both — declared once so those screens stay focused on their content. When chrome belongs to a *single*
screen, put it inline in that screen's Blade instead: a `<native:top-bar>`, `<native:bottom-nav>`, or
[`<native:fab>`](../edge-components/fab) at the root of a screen renders the same real native chrome a layout produces,
with no layout class required. See the [Top Bar](../edge-components/top-bar), [Bottom Navigation](../edge-components/bottom-nav),
and [Floating Action Button](../edge-components/fab) pages for the inline elements.

A `NativeLayout` class declares which chrome to render, and the framework automatically wraps every screen registered
under that layout with the result. Push a detail screen onto a tabs section and the chrome swaps from "tabs" to "stack"
automatically; pop back and it swaps back.

<aside>

**Which do I reach for?** Reuse across a set of screens → a layout. One screen with its own bar → inline chrome in
that screen's Blade. The two compose: a screen under a layout can still place an inline bar to override *just that
slot* for itself — see [Inline overrides](#inline-overrides). To reuse *content* (not chrome) across screens, reach
for [nested components](nested-components) instead.

</aside>

## Attaching a layout to a route

Use `Route::native(...)->layout(...)` for a single screen, or `Route::nativeGroup(...)` for a set of screens that
share the same chrome.

```php
use App\NativeComponents\Browse;
use App\NativeComponents\Home;
use App\NativeComponents\ItemDetail;
use App\NativeComponents\Layouts\StackLayout;
use App\NativeComponents\Layouts\TabsLayout;
use App\NativeComponents\Profile;

// Three screens that share a tab-bar layout
Route::nativeGroup(TabsLayout::class, function () {
    Route::native('/tabs',         Home::class);
    Route::native('/tabs/browse',  Browse::class);
    Route::native('/tabs/profile', Profile::class);
});

// One screen with a stack-style top bar (back chevron + title)
Route::native('/item/{id}', ItemDetail::class)
    ->layout(StackLayout::class);
```

A screen with no layout renders without chrome — useful for splash, onboarding, or full-bleed views.

## Built-in layouts

NativePHP doesn't ship layouts in the framework — you write your own (they're tiny, see below). The sample app
includes two reference layouts you can copy as a starting point:

- `App\NativeComponents\Layouts\StackLayout` - Back chevron + screen title. No bottom tabs.
- `App\NativeComponents\Layouts\TabsLayout` - Title bar plus a 3-tab bottom nav.

@verbatim
If you use the `nativephp/mobile-ui` plugin, its `native-ui-layouts` publish tag scaffolds a starter `<x-layouts.app>`
Blade component that wraps a screen's content with safe-area handling and optional scrolling — copy it to
`feed.blade.php`, `detail.blade.php`, and so on for multiple page archetypes.
@endverbatim

```bash
php artisan vendor:publish --tag=native-ui-layouts
```

## Writing a custom layout

Extend `Native\Mobile\Edge\Layouts\NativeLayout` and override `navBar()` and/or `tabBar()`. Returning `null` from a
method means "don't render that chrome."

```php
namespace App\NativeComponents\Layouts;

use Native\Mobile\Edge\Layouts\Builders\NavAction;
use Native\Mobile\Edge\Layouts\Builders\NavBar;
use Native\Mobile\Edge\Layouts\Builders\Tab;
use Native\Mobile\Edge\Layouts\Builders\TabBar;
use Native\Mobile\Edge\Layouts\NativeLayout;
use Native\Mobile\Edge\NativeComponent;

class SyncUpTabsLayout extends NativeLayout
{
    public function navBar(NativeComponent $screen): ?NavBar
    {
        return NavBar::make()
            ->title($screen->navTitle())
            ->subtitle('All caught up')
            ->back()
            ->backgroundColor('#0891b2')
            ->textColor('#FFFFFF')
            ->elevation(8)
            ->action(NavAction::make('search')->icon('search')->press('openSearch'));
    }

    public function tabBar(NativeComponent $screen): ?TabBar
    {
        return TabBar::make()
            ->dark()
            ->activeColor('#0891b2')
            ->labelVisibility('labeled')
            ->add(Tab::link('Chats',   '/syncup',          icon: 'chat_bubble')->badge('2'))
            ->add(Tab::link('Friends', '/syncup/friends',  icon: 'person.3.fill')->news())
            ->add(Tab::link('Profile', '/syncup/profile',  icon: 'person'));
    }
}
```

The `$screen` parameter is the live `NativeComponent` instance for the current screen, so the layout can read
properties or methods on it (such as `$screen->navTitle()`) to customize the chrome per screen.

## Builder reference

The chrome is described entirely with these fluent builders — you never place a top bar or tab bar as an element
in a screen's Blade.

Any icon you pass to these builders can also be one of your own
[custom icons](../edge-components/icon#custom-icons) <x-docs.version-badge since="4.7" />, such as
`Icon::custom('git-commit-vertical')`.

### `NavBar` — the top bar

- `make()` — create a builder
- `title(?string)` / `subtitle(?string)` — title and the small line under it
- `titleView(Element|View)` — render a custom element or Blade view in the bar's centered slot instead of the string title (a logo lockup, wordmark, …)
- `logo(string $src, float $height = 28)` — convenience over `titleView()` for a bundled logo image
- `back(bool $show = true)` — show the back chevron
- `backgroundColor(string)` / `textColor(string)` — bar background and title/icon tint
- `font(string)` — custom font for the title/subtitle: a `resources/fonts/` token or config alias (see [Chrome fonts](#chrome-fonts))
- `elevation(int $px)` — hairline thickness at the bottom of the bar
- `displayMode(string)` — `large`, `inline`, or `automatic`
- `scrollBehavior(string)` — `collapse`, `pinned`, or `enterAlways`
- `searchBar(string $placeholder = '', ?string $onQuery = null, int $debounceMs = 300)` — attach a native search bar (see [Search](../digging-deeper/search))
- `action(NavAction $action)` — append a trailing action

### `NavAction` — a top-bar button or menu

- `make(string $id)` — create an action with a unique id
- `icon(?string $name = null, ios:, android:)` — a named [icon](../edge-components/icon), optionally per-platform
- `label(string)` — visible/overflow label; `a11yLabel(string)` — screen-reader label for icon-only actions
- `press(string $method)` — screen method to call when tapped
- `url(string)` — navigate to a URL when tapped; `event(string)` — dispatch a native event (advanced)
- `destructive(bool = true)` — render in the destructive tint
- `items(array $actions)` — nest `NavAction`s to render a pull-down menu; `NavAction::divider()` adds a separator

#### Custom title view / logo

Use `logo()` for the common case — a bundled brand image in place of the string title — or `titleView()` for any
element tree or Blade view:

```php
public function navBar(NativeComponent $screen): ?NavBar
{
    return NavBar::make()
        ->logo('images/logo.png');                       // bundled asset, ~28pt tall
        // ->titleView(Image::make('images/logo.png')->height(24))
        // ->titleView(view('native.brand-lockup'))
}
```

<aside>

A custom title view takes over the bar's centered slot and forces **inline** display mode, replacing the string
title entirely. Bundle the image as an app asset rather than a remote URL so the bar doesn't flash while it loads.
On iOS it renders as a `.principal` toolbar item; on Android it fills the `TopAppBar` title slot.

</aside>

### `TabBar` — the bottom tabs

- `make()` — create a builder; `add(Tab $tab)` — append a tab (up to 5)
- `activeColor(string)` / `backgroundColor(string)` / `textColor(string)` — tab colors
- `font(string)` — custom font for tab labels: a `resources/fonts/` token or config alias (see [Chrome fonts](#chrome-fonts))
- `labelVisibility(string)` — `labeled`, `selected`, or `unlabeled`
- `dark(bool = true)` — force dark styling
- `minimizeOnScroll(bool = true)` — shrink the bar as content scrolls (iOS 26)
- `highlight(string $currentUrl)` — mark the active tab by longest-prefix URL match

### `Tab` — a tab item

- `Tab::link(string $label, string $url, icon:, ios:, android:)` — a navigating tab
- `Tab::action(string $label, icon:)` — a tab that calls a method instead of navigating
- `Tab::search(string $label, icon:, placeholder:)` — a tab that presents a search bar
- `id(string)`, `press(string $method)`, `badge(string $text, ?string $color = null)`, `news(bool = true)` (red dot), `active(bool = true)`

## Chrome fonts

Render the chrome in a custom font — a `resources/fonts/` file token or a
[config alias](../edge-components/text#font-aliases--the-app-wide-default)
like `accent` (see [Text › Custom fonts](../edge-components/text#custom-fonts);
download with `php artisan native:font`). Three tiers, most specific wins:

```php
class AppLayout extends NativeTabsLayout
{
    // 1. Layout-wide: nav bar + tab bar of every screen under this layout.
    protected ?string $font = 'accent';

    public function navBar(NativeComponent $screen): ?NavBar
    {
        // 2. Per-bar override.
        return NavBar::make()->title($screen->navTitle())->font('Inter-Bold');
    }
}

// 3. Per-screen override, from the screen itself:
public function navigationOptions(): ?NavBarOptions
{
    return NavBarOptions::make()->font('RockSalt-Regular');
}
```

Unset tiers fall through to the app-wide default font (the `fonts.default`
alias, or the older `font-family` theme token), then the system font.

<aside>

**iOS limits** (UIKit, not configurable): system-drawn **large** titles keep
the app-default font — per-layout fonts apply to inline titles and subtitles.
Tab-bar label fonts apply on iOS 25 and earlier; iOS 26 Liquid Glass bars
reject appearance overrides, so labels keep the system font there. Android
honors every tier everywhere.

</aside>

## Drawer navigation

For a slide-out side drawer, mix the mobile-ui `HasLayoutDrawer` trait into your layout and return a `Drawer` from
`drawer()`. The content is any Blade view, so you build the drawer's UI with normal EDGE components:

```php
use Native\Mobile\UI\Builders\Drawer;
use Native\Mobile\UI\Concerns\HasLayoutDrawer;

class AppLayout extends NativeLayout
{
    use HasLayoutDrawer;

    public function drawer(NativeComponent $screen): ?Drawer
    {
        return Drawer::make(view('native.sidebar'))
            ->width(320)
            ->reveal();   // ->modal() (dim + slide over) is the default
    }
}
```

### `Drawer` builder

- `make(View|Element $content)` — the drawer's content: a Blade view, or a pre-built element tree
- `width(int $points)` — drawer width in points/dp. Omit it for the platform default: ≈85% of the screen width in portrait, 40% in landscape
- `modal()` — slide the drawer over the content with a dim scrim (default)
- `reveal()` — push the main content aside to expose the drawer behind it

### Built-in interaction

The drawer is fully interactive without any wiring on your part:

- A ☰ hamburger affordance is drawn automatically at the top-leading corner while the drawer is closed, regardless of which chrome (nav bar, tab bar, or none) the screen uses.
- An edge-swipe from the left opens it; a drag back toward the edge or a tap on the scrim closes it.
- An open drawer closes automatically when you navigate to a screen whose layout has no drawer, so it never lingers over a screen that doesn't expect it.

### Per-screen drawer overrides

A single screen can replace or suppress the layout's drawer with the `InteractsWithDrawer` trait — the same shape as `navigationOptions()` for the nav bar:

```php
use Native\Mobile\UI\Builders\Drawer;
use Native\Mobile\UI\Concerns\InteractsWithDrawer;

class AdminScreen extends NativeComponent
{
    use InteractsWithDrawer;

    // Suppress the layout's drawer entirely on this screen…
    protected bool $hidesDrawer = true;

    // …or replace it just for this screen instead:
    public function drawerOverride(): ?Drawer
    {
        return Drawer::make(view('native.admin-sidebar'))->reveal();
    }
}
```

`hidesDrawer` wins outright; otherwise a non-null `drawerOverride()` beats the layout's `drawer()`, and returning `null` falls back to the layout.

## Keyboard-aware bottom content

Beyond the tab bar, a layout or an individual screen can pin its own content to the bottom of the screen — a chat
input, a search field, a contextual action bar. This content **stays above the software keyboard automatically**:
on iOS via `.safeAreaInset(.bottom)`, on Android via the `Scaffold` bottom bar plus `imePadding()`. The main
content region sits above it and keeps its own scroll.

The most ergonomic way is an inline `<native:bottom-bar>` at the root of a screen's Blade. It's lifted out of the
content flow and pinned, and it overrides the layout's `bottomBar()` for that screen:

@verbatim
```blade
<native:column class="w-full h-full">
    <native:scroll-view class="w-full flex-1">
        @foreach($messages as $message)
            <native:text class="p-3">{{ $message->body }}</native:text>
        @endforeach
    </native:scroll-view>

    {{-- Pinned to the bottom, riding above the keyboard while typing --}}
    <native:bottom-bar class="p-2 glass">
        <native:row class="w-full gap-2 items-center">
            <native:outlined-text-input native:model="draft" placeholder="Message…" class="flex-1" />
            <native:button label="Send" @press="send" />
        </native:row>
    </native:bottom-bar>
</native:column>
```
@endverbatim

To pin the same content across every screen under a layout, override `bottomBar()` instead — it returns any
element tree:

```php
public function bottomBar(NativeComponent $screen): ?Element
{
    // Return an element tree, or null for no bottom bar.
    // An inline <native:bottom-bar> on a screen overrides this for that screen.
}
```

Style the bar with the `glass` / `glass-thick` classes for a Liquid Glass capsule. Bottom-pinned content is only
rendered by layouts using native chrome (`usesNativeChrome()` is `true`).

<aside>

Let the bottom bar handle keyboard avoidance — don't add manual padding or shift the screen yourself. The platform
lifts the bar (and the content above it) when the keyboard appears; doubling that up with your own padding pushes
the content too far.

</aside>

## Floating overlay

For a pill or banner that **floats over** every screen — a "servers nearby" chip, a now-playing capsule, a
sync-status badge — mix the mobile-ui `HasFloatingOverlay` trait into your layout and return a `FloatingOverlay`
from `floatingOverlay()`. Unlike `bottomBar()`, it does **not** inset the content: it hovers on a top layer above
the content and the tab bar, so nothing is pushed up. Return `null` and nothing floats.

The content is any element tree or Blade view, so you build the overlay's UI with normal EDGE components:

```php
use Native\Mobile\UI\Builders\FloatingOverlay;
use Native\Mobile\UI\Concerns\HasFloatingOverlay;

class AppLayout extends NativeLayout
{
    use HasFloatingOverlay;

    public function floatingOverlay(NativeComponent $screen): ?FloatingOverlay
    {
        if (NearbyServers::none()) {
            return null;                                  // nothing floats
        }

        return FloatingOverlay::make(view('native.servers-pill'))
            ->offset(88);          // clearance above the tab bar; ->top() pins below the nav bar instead
    }
}
```

<aside>

Because it floats over **every** screen under the layout, the overlay's content should read from app-wide state (a
store / singleton), not the active screen's own properties — `floatingOverlay()` is re-evaluated on each publish
from the current `$screen`. A single screen can replace or suppress it with the `InteractsWithFloatingOverlay`
trait. Only rendered by layouts using native chrome (`usesNativeChrome()` is `true`).

</aside>

### `FloatingOverlay` builder

- `make(View|Element $content)` — the floating content: a Blade view, or a pre-built element tree
- `bottom()` — float against the bottom edge, above the tab bar (default)
- `top()` — float against the top edge, below the nav bar
- `offset(int $points)` — extra distance between the overlay and its aligned edge, added on top of the safe-area inset. Omit it for the platform default that clears a standard bottom tab bar; a tab-less stack layout has no tab bar to clear, so pass a small value there instead

### Per-screen overlay overrides

A single screen replaces or suppresses the layout's overlay with the `InteractsWithFloatingOverlay` trait:

```php
use Native\Mobile\UI\Builders\FloatingOverlay;
use Native\Mobile\UI\Concerns\InteractsWithFloatingOverlay;

class CheckoutScreen extends NativeComponent
{
    use InteractsWithFloatingOverlay;

    // Hide the app-wide pill on this screen…
    protected bool $hidesFloatingOverlay = true;

    // …or replace it just for this one instead:
    public function floatingOverlayOverride(): ?FloatingOverlay
    {
        return FloatingOverlay::make(view('native.checkout-hint'));
    }
}
```

`hidesFloatingOverlay` wins outright; otherwise a non-null `floatingOverlayOverride()` beats the layout's `floatingOverlay()`, and returning `null` falls back to the layout.

## How chrome wraps the screen

When a screen renders, the framework's `wrapWithChrome` flow:

1. Looks up the layout class declared on the route.
2. Calls `$layout->navBar($screen)` and `$layout->tabBar($screen)`.
3. Merges in any `navigationOptions()` declared on the screen.
4. Merges in any imperative state set via `$this->setNavBar([...])` / `$this->setTabBar([...])`.
5. Wraps the screen content in a `Column` filling the screen, with the bars stacked above and below the content.
6. Picks the right safe-area variant for the wrapper:
    - **TabBar present** → wrapper uses `safeAreaTop()`; the bar handles its own bottom inset.
    - **NavBar without TabBar** → wrapper uses `safeAreaBottom()`; the NavBar handles its own top inset.
    - **No bars** → wrapper uses `safeArea()` for both edges.

The resulting element tree looks like:

```
Column.fill().safeAreaTop()  ← (or whichever variant applies)
├─ TopBar          ← navBar
├─ <screen content> (flex-grow: 1)
└─ BottomNav       ← tabBar
```

Don't apply `safe-area` to the root of a screen wrapped by a layout — the layout already handles it.

## Per-screen NavBar contributions

Screens can add actions or override the title without writing their own layout, by implementing
`navigationOptions()`:

```php
use Native\Mobile\Edge\Layouts\Builders\NavAction;
use Native\Mobile\Edge\Layouts\Builders\NavBarOptions;
use Native\Mobile\Edge\NativeComponent;

class ItemDetail extends NativeComponent
{
    public function navigationOptions(): ?NavBarOptions
    {
        return NavBarOptions::make()
            ->title("Item #{$this->param('id')}")
            ->action(NavAction::make('save')->icon('save')->press('save'));
    }

    public function save(): void
    {
        // ...
    }
}
```

Non-null fields on the returned `NavBarOptions` override the layout's defaults; null fields fall through. Actions
are appended to whatever the layout already declared.

A screen can also opt out of the layout's nav bar entirely — the full-bleed pattern for photo viewers, onboarding
flows, and video screens:

```php
class PhotoViewer extends NativeComponent
{
    protected bool $hidesNavBar = true;
}
```

This is equivalent to returning `NavBarOptions::make()->hidden()` from `navigationOptions()`; if both are set, the
explicit builder wins. It mirrors the tab bar's `$hidesTabBar` / `tabBarOptions()->hidden()`. See
[Hiding the nav bar on a screen](../edge-components/top-bar#hiding-the-nav-bar-on-a-screen) for details.

## Per-screen titles

Override `navTitle()` to give a screen its own title that the layout's `NavBar` can read:

```php
class Profile extends NativeComponent
{
    public function navTitle(): string
    {
        return 'My Profile';
    }
}
```

5	
6	## Overview
7	
8	Native screens form a stack, exactly like a native iOS `UINavigationController` or an Android Activity stack. From
9	inside a `NativeComponent`, you push, pop, and replace screens using methods on `$this`.
10	
11	## Registering routes
12	
13	Native routes are registered similarly to Livewire routes, but instead of using `Route::livewire()` you use the
14	`Route::native()` macro:
15	
16	```php
17	use App\NativeComponents\Home;
18	use App\NativeComponents\ItemDetail;
19	
20	Route::native('/', Home::class);
21	Route::native('/item/{id}', ItemDetail::class);
22	```
23	
24	You can put these routes anywhere that makes sense for your application, but you may find that creating a
25	`routes/mobile.php` to keep them all together is a clean option.
26	
27	Route parameters work just like Laravel web routes — `{id}` matches a path segment and is exposed to the screen
28	through `$this->param('id')`.
29	
30	See [Layouts](layouts) for how to attach shared chrome to a route or group of routes, and
31	[Middleware](middleware) for guarding screens with `->middleware()`.
32	
33	## Pushing a new screen
34	
35	```php
36	$this->navigate('/item/42');
37	```
38	
39	By default a push slides in from the right. Pass arbitrary data along with the navigation:
40	
41	```php
42	$this->navigate('/item/42', ['source' => 'home-feed']);
43	```
44	
45	The next screen reads the data with `$this->data('source')`.
46	
47	## Going back
48	
49	```php
50	$this->back();
51	```
52	
53	Pops the current screen off the stack and returns to whatever was beneath it. The default transition is a slide-out
54	to the right.
55	
56	## Replacing the current screen
57	
58	```php
59	$this->replace('/login');
60	```
61	
62	Pops the current screen and pushes a new one in its place — useful after sign-in / sign-out or for in-place tab
63	swaps. The default transition is a fade.
64	
65	<aside>
66	
67	`<native:bottom-nav-item>` taps automatically use `replace` semantics, so the back chevron pops the entire tabs
68	section in one step rather than stepping through tab history.
69	
70	</aside>
71	
72	## Exiting to the web view
73	
74	```php
75	$this->exitToWeb('/dashboard');
76	```
77	
78	Tear down the native UI stack and load the given URL in the web view. Use this for screens that aren't part of the
79	native experience.
80	
81	## Custom transitions
82	
83	Chain `transition()` after a navigation method to override the default animation:
84	
85	```php
86	use Native\Mobile\Edge\Transition;
87	
88	$this->navigate('/item/42')->transition(Transition::SlideFromBottom);
89	```
90	
91	Available cases:
92	
93	- `Transition::SlideFromRight` - default for `navigate()`
94	- `Transition::SlideFromLeft` - default for `back()`
95	- `Transition::SlideFromBottom` - modal-style presentation
96	- `Transition::Fade` - default for `replace()`
97	- `Transition::FadeFromBottom` - subtle vertical fade
98	- `Transition::ScaleFromCenter` - zoom-in effect
99	- `Transition::ParallaxPush` - incoming screen slides in from the right while the outgoing screen drifts partially left underneath
100	- `Transition::Morph` <x-docs.version-badge since="4.7" /> - cross-fade while elements that share a `ref` move between the two screens. See [Morphing elements between screens](#morphing-elements-between-screens)
101	- `Transition::None` - swap with no animation
102	
103	## Navigating from Blade
104	
105	The `@navigate` directive triggers navigation directly from your view, with no component method required. It works on
106	any node, so any element can become a navigation target.
107	
108	The short form takes a route in single quotes:
109	
110	@verbatim
111	```blade
112	<native:pressable @navigate='/item/42' class="w-full p-4">
113	    <native:text>View item</native:text>
114	</native:pressable>
115	```
116	@endverbatim
117	
118	To pass data along with the navigation, use the args form — a route followed by an array:
119	
120	@verbatim
121	```blade
122	<native:pressable @navigate="'/item/42', ['source' => 'home-feed']">
123	    <native:text>View item</native:text>
124	</native:pressable>
125	```
126	@endverbatim
127	
128	The next screen reads the data with `$this->data('source')`, exactly as with `$this->navigate()`.
129	
130	Double quotes hold a PHP expression rather than a plain route, so `@navigate="/item/42"` won't compile. For a
131	dynamic route, build the string in PHP: `@navigate="'/item/' . $item->id"`.
132	
133	### Transition modifiers
134	
135	Add a transition as a modifier to override the default push animation:
136	
137	@verbatim
138	```blade
139	<native:pressable @navigate.slideFromBottom='/item/42'>
140	    <native:text>Present modally</native:text>
141	</native:pressable>
142	```
143	@endverbatim
144	
145	Available transition modifiers:
146	
147	- `fade`
148	- `slideFromRight`
149	- `slideFromLeft`
150	- `slideFromBottom`
151	- `fadeFromBottom`
152	- `scaleFromCenter`
153	- `parallaxPush`
154	- `morph` <x-docs.version-badge since="4.7" />
155	- `none`
156	
157	### Action modifiers
158	
159	Modifiers also select the navigation action. Use these in place of a route to `back`, or combine them with a route
160	to `replace` or `exitToWeb`:
161	
162	@verbatim
163	```blade
164	<native:pressable @navigate.back>
165	    <native:text>Go back</native:text>
166	</native:pressable>
167	
168	<native:pressable @navigate.replace='/login'>
169	    <native:text>Sign out</native:text>
170	</native:pressable>
171	
172	<native:pressable @navigate.exitToWeb='/dashboard'>
173	    <native:text>Open dashboard</native:text>
174	</native:pressable>
175	```
176	@endverbatim
177	
178	Transition and action modifiers can be combined — `@navigate.replace.fade='/login'`.
179	
180	## Morphing elements between screens
181	
182	<x-docs.version-badge since="4.7" />
183	
184	The morph transition carries an element from where it sits on one screen to where it sits on the next. A thumbnail
185	grows into a header image, or an avatar slides into place on a profile page. If you've used the web's View
186	Transitions API, it's the same idea.
187	
188	Give the element the same `ref` on both screens, then navigate with the `morph` modifier:
189	
190	@verbatim
191	```blade
192	{{-- The album list --}}
193	@foreach ($albums as $album)
194	    <native:pressable @navigate.morph="'/album/' . $album->id">
195	        <native:image :ref="'album-' . $album->id" :src="$album->cover" class="w-16 h-16 rounded-xl" />
196	    </native:pressable>
197	@endforeach
198	```
199	@endverbatim
200	
201	@verbatim
202	```blade
203	{{-- The album screen --}}
204	<native:column class="w-full">
205	    <native:image :ref="'album-' . $album->id" :src="$album->cover" class="w-full h-80" />
206	
207	    <native:pressable @navigate.back.morph>
208	        <native:text>Back</native:text>
209	    </native:pressable>
210	</native:column>
211	```
212	@endverbatim
213	
214	Tapping an album cross-fades the two screens while the cover moves and grows from the small tile into the header.
215	Going back with `@navigate.back.morph` plays it in reverse.
216	
217	From a component, pass `Transition::Morph`:
218	
219	```php
220	use Native\Mobile\Edge\Transition;
221	
222	$this->navigate('/album/3')->transition(Transition::Morph);
223	```
224	
225	### Shaping the morph
226	
227	These attributes change how an element travels. They're read from the element on the screen you're navigating to,
228	so put them on both elements if you want the same motion in both directions.
229	
230	- `morph` - what moves. `frame` (the default) moves and resizes the element. `position` moves it at its final size.
231	  `size` resizes it in place, at its final position. `none` stops the element morphing.
232	- `morph-duration` - length in milliseconds. The default is `350`, the same as the cross-fade behind it.
233	- `morph-easing` - the curve: `linear`, `ease-in`, `ease-out`, `ease-in-out` (the default) or `spring`.
234	
235	@verbatim
236	```blade
237	<native:column ref="now-playing" morph="position" morph-duration="500" morph-easing="spring">
238	    ...
239	</native:column>
240	```
241	@endverbatim
242	
243	<aside>
244	
245	On Android, `position` and `size` behave like `frame`. Compose's shared element API always animates the whole frame,
246	so the element moves and resizes together.
247	
248	</aside>
249	
250	### Which elements morph
251	
252	- An element morphs only when its `ref` is on both screens. Everything else cross-fades with its screen.
253	- Elements only morph under the `morph` transition. A `ref` that appears on both screens does nothing during a slide
254	  or a fade.
255	- Keep each `ref` unique within a screen. If two elements share one, you can't be sure which of them moves.
256	- `ref` is also how [tests target elements](../testing/interactions#by-ref). If you've reused a test `ref` on two
257	  screens and don't want those elements to morph, add `morph="none"` to either of them.
258	
259	### Native chrome
260	
261	A morph needs one whole screen to replace another. Inside native chrome that doesn't always happen. Pushing from one
262	screen with a native top bar to another, or switching between tabs of a bottom nav, is animated by the platform's
263	own navigation, and nothing morphs.
264	
265	Morphs do run between screens that have no native chrome, and whenever the chrome changes, such as a tab screen
266	opening a detail screen that has a top bar instead. See [Layouts](layouts) for how screens get their chrome.
267	
268	## Reading params and data
269	
270	```php
271	class ItemDetail extends NativeComponent
272	{
273	    public function mount(): void
274	    {
275	        $id = $this->param('id');                  // from the route URI
276	        $source = $this->data('source', 'unknown'); // from navigate()'s second arg
277	
278	        // ...
279	    }
280	}
281	```
282	
283	Both accessors take an optional default that's returned when the key is missing.
284	
285	## Resolving named routes
286	
287	If you've named your routes you can use `route()` on the component to resolve them to URIs:
288	
289	```php
290	$this->navigate($this->route('listing.show', ['id' => 5]));
291	```
292	
293	This delegates to Laravel's URL generator with `absolute: false`.
294	
295	## Customizing device-back behavior
296	
297	By default, the device back button (Android) pops the navigation stack. Override `onBackPressed()` to add custom
298	behavior:
299	
300	```php
301	class CheckoutForm extends NativeComponent
302	{
303	    public bool $dirty = false;
304	
305	    public function onBackPressed(): void
306	    {
307	        if ($this->dirty) {
308	            $this->showDiscardConfirmation();
309	
310	            return;
311	        }
312	
313	        $this->back();
314	    }
315	}
316	```
317	
318	If the back press should ultimately still pop, call `$this->back()` from your override.

323	
324	## Overview
325	
326	Layouts are **optional**. They're the tool for chrome that's shared across *many* screens — a top nav bar, a bottom
327	tab bar, or both — declared once so those screens stay focused on their content. When chrome belongs to a *single*
328	screen, put it inline in that screen's Blade instead: a `<native:top-bar>`, `<native:bottom-nav>`, or
329	[`<native:fab>`](../edge-components/fab) at the root of a screen renders the same real native chrome a layout produces,
330	with no layout class required. See the [Top Bar](../edge-components/top-bar), [Bottom Navigation](../edge-components/bottom-nav),
331	and [Floating Action Button](../edge-components/fab) pages for the inline elements.
332	
333	A `NativeLayout` class declares which chrome to render, and the framework automatically wraps every screen registered
334	under that layout with the result. Push a detail screen onto a tabs section and the chrome swaps from "tabs" to "stack"
335	automatically; pop back and it swaps back.
336	
337	<aside>
338	
339	**Which do I reach for?** Reuse across a set of screens → a layout. One screen with its own bar → inline chrome in
340	that screen's Blade. The two compose: a screen under a layout can still place an inline bar to override *just that
341	slot* for itself — see [Inline overrides](#inline-overrides). To reuse *content* (not chrome) across screens, reach
342	for [nested components](nested-components) instead.
343	
344	</aside>
345	
346	## Attaching a layout to a route
347	
348	Use `Route::native(...)->layout(...)` for a single screen, or `Route::nativeGroup(...)` for a set of screens that
349	share the same chrome.
350	
351	```php
352	use App\NativeComponents\Browse;
353	use App\NativeComponents\Home;
354	use App\NativeComponents\ItemDetail;
355	use App\NativeComponents\Layouts\StackLayout;
356	use App\NativeComponents\Layouts\TabsLayout;
357	use App\NativeComponents\Profile;
358	
359	// Three screens that share a tab-bar layout
360	Route::nativeGroup(TabsLayout::class, function () {
361	    Route::native('/tabs',         Home::class);
362	    Route::native('/tabs/browse',  Browse::class);
363	    Route::native('/tabs/profile', Profile::class);
364	});
365	
366	// One screen with a stack-style top bar (back chevron + title)
367	Route::native('/item/{id}', ItemDetail::class)
368	    ->layout(StackLayout::class);
369	```
370	
371	A screen with no layout renders without chrome — useful for splash, onboarding, or full-bleed views.
372	
373	## Built-in layouts
374	
375	NativePHP doesn't ship layouts in the framework — you write your own (they're tiny, see below). The sample app
376	includes two reference layouts you can copy as a starting point:
377	
378	- `App\NativeComponents\Layouts\StackLayout` - Back chevron + screen title. No bottom tabs.
379	- `App\NativeComponents\Layouts\TabsLayout` - Title bar plus a 3-tab bottom nav.
380	
381	@verbatim
382	If you use the `nativephp/mobile-ui` plugin, its `native-ui-layouts` publish tag scaffolds a starter `<x-layouts.app>`
383	Blade component that wraps a screen's content with safe-area handling and optional scrolling — copy it to
384	`feed.blade.php`, `detail.blade.php`, and so on for multiple page archetypes.
385	@endverbatim
386	
387	```bash
388	php artisan vendor:publish --tag=native-ui-layouts
389	```
390	
391	## Writing a custom layout
392	
393	Extend `Native\Mobile\Edge\Layouts\NativeLayout` and override `navBar()` and/or `tabBar()`. Returning `null` from a
394	method means "don't render that chrome."
395	
396	```php
397	namespace App\NativeComponents\Layouts;
398	
399	use Native\Mobile\Edge\Layouts\Builders\NavAction;
400	use Native\Mobile\Edge\Layouts\Builders\NavBar;
401	use Native\Mobile\Edge\Layouts\Builders\Tab;
402	use Native\Mobile\Edge\Layouts\Builders\TabBar;
403	use Native\Mobile\Edge\Layouts\NativeLayout;
404	use Native\Mobile\Edge\NativeComponent;
405	
406	class SyncUpTabsLayout extends NativeLayout
407	{
408	    public function navBar(NativeComponent $screen): ?NavBar
409	    {
410	        return NavBar::make()
411	            ->title($screen->navTitle())
412	            ->subtitle('All caught up')
413	            ->back()
414	            ->backgroundColor('#0891b2')
415	            ->textColor('#FFFFFF')
416	            ->elevation(8)
417	            ->action(NavAction::make('search')->icon('search')->press('openSearch'));
418	    }
419	
420	    public function tabBar(NativeComponent $screen): ?TabBar
421	    {
422	        return TabBar::make()
423	            ->dark()
424	            ->activeColor('#0891b2')
425	            ->labelVisibility('labeled')
426	            ->add(Tab::link('Chats',   '/syncup',          icon: 'chat_bubble')->badge('2'))
427	            ->add(Tab::link('Friends', '/syncup/friends',  icon: 'person.3.fill')->news())
428	            ->add(Tab::link('Profile', '/syncup/profile',  icon: 'person'));
429	    }
430	}
431	```
432	
433	The `$screen` parameter is the live `NativeComponent` instance for the current screen, so the layout can read
434	properties or methods on it (such as `$screen->navTitle()`) to customize the chrome per screen.
435	
436	## Builder reference
437	
438	The chrome is described entirely with these fluent builders — you never place a top bar or tab bar as an element
439	in a screen's Blade.
440	
441	Any icon you pass to these builders can also be one of your own
442	[custom icons](../edge-components/icon#custom-icons) <x-docs.version-badge since="4.7" />, such as
443	`Icon::custom('git-commit-vertical')`.
444	
445	### `NavBar` — the top bar
446	
447	- `make()` — create a builder
448	- `title(?string)` / `subtitle(?string)` — title and the small line under it
449	- `titleView(Element|View)` — render a custom element or Blade view in the bar's centered slot instead of the string title (a logo lockup, wordmark, …)
450	- `logo(string $src, float $height = 28)` — convenience over `titleView()` for a bundled logo image
451	- `back(bool $show = true)` — show the back chevron
452	- `backgroundColor(string)` / `textColor(string)` — bar background and title/icon tint
453	- `font(string)` — custom font for the title/subtitle: a `resources/fonts/` token or config alias (see [Chrome fonts](#chrome-fonts))
454	- `elevation(int $px)` — hairline thickness at the bottom of the bar
455	- `displayMode(string)` — `large`, `inline`, or `automatic`
456	- `scrollBehavior(string)` — `collapse`, `pinned`, or `enterAlways`
457	- `searchBar(string $placeholder = '', ?string $onQuery = null, int $debounceMs = 300)` — attach a native search bar (see [Search](../digging-deeper/search))
458	- `action(NavAction $action)` — append a trailing action
459	
460	### `NavAction` — a top-bar button or menu
461	
462	- `make(string $id)` — create an action with a unique id
463	- `icon(?string $name = null, ios:, android:)` — a named [icon](../edge-components/icon), optionally per-platform
464	- `label(string)` — visible/overflow label; `a11yLabel(string)` — screen-reader label for icon-only actions
465	- `press(string $method)` — screen method to call when tapped
466	- `url(string)` — navigate to a URL when tapped; `event(string)` — dispatch a native event (advanced)
467	- `destructive(bool = true)` — render in the destructive tint
468	- `items(array $actions)` — nest `NavAction`s to render a pull-down menu; `NavAction::divider()` adds a separator
469	
470	#### Custom title view / logo
471	
472	Use `logo()` for the common case — a bundled brand image in place of the string title — or `titleView()` for any
473	element tree or Blade view:
474	
475	```php
476	public function navBar(NativeComponent $screen): ?NavBar
477	{
478	    return NavBar::make()
479	        ->logo('images/logo.png');                       // bundled asset, ~28pt tall
480	        // ->titleView(Image::make('images/logo.png')->height(24))
481	        // ->titleView(view('native.brand-lockup'))
482	}
483	```
484	
485	<aside>
486	
487	A custom title view takes over the bar's centered slot and forces **inline** display mode, replacing the string
488	title entirely. Bundle the image as an app asset rather than a remote URL so the bar doesn't flash while it loads.
489	On iOS it renders as a `.principal` toolbar item; on Android it fills the `TopAppBar` title slot.
490	
491	</aside>
492	
493	### `TabBar` — the bottom tabs
494	
495	- `make()` — create a builder; `add(Tab $tab)` — append a tab (up to 5)
496	- `activeColor(string)` / `backgroundColor(string)` / `textColor(string)` — tab colors
497	- `font(string)` — custom font for tab labels: a `resources/fonts/` token or config alias (see [Chrome fonts](#chrome-fonts))
498	- `labelVisibility(string)` — `labeled`, `selected`, or `unlabeled`
499	- `dark(bool = true)` — force dark styling
500	- `minimizeOnScroll(bool = true)` — shrink the bar as content scrolls (iOS 26)
501	- `highlight(string $currentUrl)` — mark the active tab by longest-prefix URL match
502	
503	### `Tab` — a tab item
504	
505	- `Tab::link(string $label, string $url, icon:, ios:, android:)` — a navigating tab
506	- `Tab::action(string $label, icon:)` — a tab that calls a method instead of navigating
507	- `Tab::search(string $label, icon:, placeholder:)` — a tab that presents a search bar
508	- `id(string)`, `press(string $method)`, `badge(string $text, ?string $color = null)`, `news(bool = true)` (red dot), `active(bool = true)`
509	
510	## Chrome fonts
511	
512	Render the chrome in a custom font — a `resources/fonts/` file token or a
513	[config alias](../edge-components/text#font-aliases--the-app-wide-default)
514	like `accent` (see [Text › Custom fonts](../edge-components/text#custom-fonts);
515	download with `php artisan native:font`). Three tiers, most specific wins:
516	
517	```php
518	class AppLayout extends NativeTabsLayout
519	{
520	    // 1. Layout-wide: nav bar + tab bar of every screen under this layout.
521	    protected ?string $font = 'accent';
522	
523	    public function navBar(NativeComponent $screen): ?NavBar
524	    {
525	        // 2. Per-bar override.
526	        return NavBar::make()->title($screen->navTitle())->font('Inter-Bold');
527	    }
528	}
529	
530	// 3. Per-screen override, from the screen itself:
531	public function navigationOptions(): ?NavBarOptions
532	{
533	    return NavBarOptions::make()->font('RockSalt-Regular');
534	}
535	```
536	
537	Unset tiers fall through to the app-wide default font (the `fonts.default`
538	alias, or the older `font-family` theme token), then the system font.
539	
540	<aside>
541	
542	**iOS limits** (UIKit, not configurable): system-drawn **large** titles keep
543	the app-default font — per-layout fonts apply to inline titles and subtitles.
544	Tab-bar label fonts apply on iOS 25 and earlier; iOS 26 Liquid Glass bars
545	reject appearance overrides, so labels keep the system font there. Android
546	honors every tier everywhere.
547	
548	</aside>
549	
550	## Drawer navigation
551	
552	For a slide-out side drawer, mix the mobile-ui `HasLayoutDrawer` trait into your layout and return a `Drawer` from
553	`drawer()`. The content is any Blade view, so you build the drawer's UI with normal EDGE components:
554	
555	```php
556	use Native\Mobile\UI\Builders\Drawer;
557	use Native\Mobile\UI\Concerns\HasLayoutDrawer;
558	
559	class AppLayout extends NativeLayout
560	{
561	    use HasLayoutDrawer;
562	
563	    public function drawer(NativeComponent $screen): ?Drawer
564	    {
565	        return Drawer::make(view('native.sidebar'))
566	            ->width(320)
567	            ->reveal();   // ->modal() (dim + slide over) is the default
568	    }
569	}
570	```
571	
572	### `Drawer` builder
573	
574	- `make(View|Element $content)` — the drawer's content: a Blade view, or a pre-built element tree
575	- `width(int $points)` — drawer width in points/dp. Omit it for the platform default: ≈85% of the screen width in portrait, 40% in landscape
576	- `modal()` — slide the drawer over the content with a dim scrim (default)
577	- `reveal()` — push the main content aside to expose the drawer behind it
578	
579	### Built-in interaction
580	
581	The drawer is fully interactive without any wiring on your part:
582	
583	- A ☰ hamburger affordance is drawn automatically at the top-leading corner while the drawer is closed, regardless of which chrome (nav bar, tab bar, or none) the screen uses.
584	- An edge-swipe from the left opens it; a drag back toward the edge or a tap on the scrim closes it.
585	- An open drawer closes automatically when you navigate to a screen whose layout has no drawer, so it never lingers over a screen that doesn't expect it.
586	
587	### Per-screen drawer overrides
588	
589	A single screen can replace or suppress the layout's drawer with the `InteractsWithDrawer` trait — the same shape as `navigationOptions()` for the nav bar:
590	
591	```php
592	use Native\Mobile\UI\Builders\Drawer;
593	use Native\Mobile\UI\Concerns\InteractsWithDrawer;
594	
595	class AdminScreen extends NativeComponent
596	{
597	    use InteractsWithDrawer;
598	
599	    // Suppress the layout's drawer entirely on this screen…
600	    protected bool $hidesDrawer = true;
601	
602	    // …or replace it just for this screen instead:
603	    public function drawerOverride(): ?Drawer
604	    {
605	        return Drawer::make(view('native.admin-sidebar'))->reveal();
606	    }
607	}
608	```
609	
610	`hidesDrawer` wins outright; otherwise a non-null `drawerOverride()` beats the layout's `drawer()`, and returning `null` falls back to the layout.
611	
612	## Keyboard-aware bottom content
613	
614	Beyond the tab bar, a layout or an individual screen can pin its own content to the bottom of the screen — a chat
615	input, a search field, a contextual action bar. This content **stays above the software keyboard automatically**:
616	on iOS via `.safeAreaInset(.bottom)`, on Android via the `Scaffold` bottom bar plus `imePadding()`. The main
617	content region sits above it and keeps its own scroll.
618	
619	The most ergonomic way is an inline `<native:bottom-bar>` at the root of a screen's Blade. It's lifted out of the
620	content flow and pinned, and it overrides the layout's `bottomBar()` for that screen:
621	
622	@verbatim
623	```blade
624	<native:column class="w-full h-full">
625	    <native:scroll-view class="w-full flex-1">
626	        @foreach($messages as $message)
627	            <native:text class="p-3">{{ $message->body }}</native:text>
628	        @endforeach
629	    </native:scroll-view>
630	
631	    {{-- Pinned to the bottom, riding above the keyboard while typing --}}
632	    <native:bottom-bar class="p-2 glass">
633	        <native:row class="w-full gap-2 items-center">
634	            <native:outlined-text-input native:model="draft" placeholder="Message…" class="flex-1" />
635	            <native:button label="Send" @press="send" />
636	        </native:row>
637	    </native:bottom-bar>
638	</native:column>
639	```
640	@endverbatim
641	
642	To pin the same content across every screen under a layout, override `bottomBar()` instead — it returns any
643	element tree:
644	
645	```php
646	public function bottomBar(NativeComponent $screen): ?Element
647	{
648	    // Return an element tree, or null for no bottom bar.
649	    // An inline <native:bottom-bar> on a screen overrides this for that screen.
650	}
651	```
652	
653	Style the bar with the `glass` / `glass-thick` classes for a Liquid Glass capsule. Bottom-pinned content is only
654	rendered by layouts using native chrome (`usesNativeChrome()` is `true`).
655	
656	<aside>
657	
658	Let the bottom bar handle keyboard avoidance — don't add manual padding or shift the screen yourself. The platform
659	lifts the bar (and the content above it) when the keyboard appears; doubling that up with your own padding pushes
660	the content too far.
661	
662	</aside>
663	
664	## Floating overlay
665	
666	For a pill or banner that **floats over** every screen — a "servers nearby" chip, a now-playing capsule, a
667	sync-status badge — mix the mobile-ui `HasFloatingOverlay` trait into your layout and return a `FloatingOverlay`
668	from `floatingOverlay()`. Unlike `bottomBar()`, it does **not** inset the content: it hovers on a top layer above
669	the content and the tab bar, so nothing is pushed up. Return `null` and nothing floats.
670	
671	The content is any element tree or Blade view, so you build the overlay's UI with normal EDGE components:
672	
673	```php
674	use Native\Mobile\UI\Builders\FloatingOverlay;
675	use Native\Mobile\UI\Concerns\HasFloatingOverlay;
676	
677	class AppLayout extends NativeLayout
678	{
679	    use HasFloatingOverlay;
680	
681	    public function floatingOverlay(NativeComponent $screen): ?FloatingOverlay
682	    {
683	        if (NearbyServers::none()) {
684	            return null;                                  // nothing floats
685	        }
686	
687	        return FloatingOverlay::make(view('native.servers-pill'))
688	            ->offset(88);          // clearance above the tab bar; ->top() pins below the nav bar instead
689	    }
690	}
691	```
692	
693	<aside>
694	
695	Because it floats over **every** screen under the layout, the overlay's content should read from app-wide state (a
696	store / singleton), not the active screen's own properties — `floatingOverlay()` is re-evaluated on each publish
697	from the current `$screen`. A single screen can replace or suppress it with the `InteractsWithFloatingOverlay`
698	trait. Only rendered by layouts using native chrome (`usesNativeChrome()` is `true`).
699	
700	</aside>
701	
702	### `FloatingOverlay` builder
703	
704	- `make(View|Element $content)` — the floating content: a Blade view, or a pre-built element tree
705	- `bottom()` — float against the bottom edge, above the tab bar (default)
706	- `top()` — float against the top edge, below the nav bar
707	- `offset(int $points)` — extra distance between the overlay and its aligned edge, added on top of the safe-area inset. Omit it for the platform default that clears a standard bottom tab bar; a tab-less stack layout has no tab bar to clear, so pass a small value there instead
708	
709	### Per-screen overlay overrides
710	
711	A single screen replaces or suppresses the layout's overlay with the `InteractsWithFloatingOverlay` trait:
712	
713	```php
714	use Native\Mobile\UI\Builders\FloatingOverlay;
715	use Native\Mobile\UI\Concerns\InteractsWithFloatingOverlay;
716	
717	class CheckoutScreen extends NativeComponent
718	{
719	    use InteractsWithFloatingOverlay;
720	
721	    // Hide the app-wide pill on this screen…
722	    protected bool $hidesFloatingOverlay = true;
723	
724	    // …or replace it just for this one instead:
725	    public function floatingOverlayOverride(): ?FloatingOverlay
726	    {
727	        return FloatingOverlay::make(view('native.checkout-hint'));
728	    }
729	}
730	```
731	
732	`hidesFloatingOverlay` wins outright; otherwise a non-null `floatingOverlayOverride()` beats the layout's `floatingOverlay()`, and returning `null` falls back to the layout.
733	
734	## How chrome wraps the screen
735	
736	When a screen renders, the framework's `wrapWithChrome` flow:
737	
738	1. Looks up the layout class declared on the route.
739	2. Calls `$layout->navBar($screen)` and `$layout->tabBar($screen)`.
740	3. Merges in any `navigationOptions()` declared on the screen.
741	4. Merges in any imperative state set via `$this->setNavBar([...])` / `$this->setTabBar([...])`.
742	5. Wraps the screen content in a `Column` filling the screen, with the bars stacked above and below the content.
743	6. Picks the right safe-area variant for the wrapper:
744	    - **TabBar present** → wrapper uses `safeAreaTop()`; the bar handles its own bottom inset.
745	    - **NavBar without TabBar** → wrapper uses `safeAreaBottom()`; the NavBar handles its own top inset.
746	    - **No bars** → wrapper uses `safeArea()` for both edges.
747	
748	The resulting element tree looks like:
749	
750	```
751	Column.fill().safeAreaTop()  ← (or whichever variant applies)
752	├─ TopBar          ← navBar
753	├─ <screen content> (flex-grow: 1)
754	└─ BottomNav       ← tabBar
755	```
756	
757	Don't apply `safe-area` to the root of a screen wrapped by a layout — the layout already handles it.
758	
759	## Per-screen NavBar contributions
760	
761	Screens can add actions or override the title without writing their own layout, by implementing
762	`navigationOptions()`:
763	
764	```php
765	use Native\Mobile\Edge\Layouts\Builders\NavAction;
766	use Native\Mobile\Edge\Layouts\Builders\NavBarOptions;
767	use Native\Mobile\Edge\NativeComponent;
768	
769	class ItemDetail extends NativeComponent
770	{
771	    public function navigationOptions(): ?NavBarOptions
772	    {
773	        return NavBarOptions::make()
774	            ->title("Item #{$this->param('id')}")
775	            ->action(NavAction::make('save')->icon('save')->press('save'));
776	    }
777	
778	    public function save(): void
779	    {
780	        // ...
781	    }
782	}
783	```
784	
785	Non-null fields on the returned `NavBarOptions` override the layout's defaults; null fields fall through. Actions
786	are appended to whatever the layout already declared.
787	
788	A screen can also opt out of the layout's nav bar entirely — the full-bleed pattern for photo viewers, onboarding
789	flows, and video screens:
790	
791	```php
792	class PhotoViewer extends NativeComponent
793	{
794	    protected bool $hidesNavBar = true;
795	}
796	```
797	
798	This is equivalent to returning `NavBarOptions::make()->hidden()` from `navigationOptions()`; if both are set, the
799	explicit builder wins. It mirrors the tab bar's `$hidesTabBar` / `tabBarOptions()->hidden()`. See
800	[Hiding the nav bar on a screen](../edge-components/top-bar#hiding-the-nav-bar-on-a-screen) for details.
801	
802	## Per-screen titles
803	
804	Override `navTitle()` to give a screen its own title that the layout's `NavBar` can read:
805	
806	```php
807	class Profile extends NativeComponent
808	{
809	    public function navTitle(): string
810	    {
811	        return 'My Profile';
812	    }
813	}
814	```
815	
816	A `StackLayout` that calls `->title($screen->navTitle())` will then show "My Profile" automatically when this screen
817	is on top.
818	
819	## Imperative state changes
820	
821	If you need to mutate the chrome at runtime — for example, to flip the title between "Edit" and "Done" — call
822	`$this->setNavBar([...])` or `$this->setTabBar([...])`:
823	
824	```php
825	class Notes extends NativeComponent
826	{
827	    public bool $editing = false;
828	
829	    public function toggleEdit(): void
830	    {
831	        $this->editing = ! $this->editing;
832	
833	        $this->setNavBar([
834	            'title' => $this->editing ? 'Editing' : 'Notes',
835	        ]);
836	    }
837	}
838	```
839	
840	Imperative state is merged onto the layout's NavBar at the next render. Supported keys mirror the `NavBar` builder
841	methods: `title`, `subtitle`, `back`, `backgroundColor`, `textColor`, `elevation`.
842	
843	## Inline overrides
844	
845	Inline chrome and a layout compose. A screen can put its own [`<native:top-bar>`](../edge-components/top-bar) or
846	[`<native:bottom-nav>`](../edge-components/bottom-nav) at the root of its Blade, and the framework skips the
847	layout-supplied chrome **for that slot only** — the *other* slot still comes from the layout. This is the override
848	contract for one-off screens (a chat detail with a custom titled top bar, say) without dropping the layout entirely.
849	
850	@verbatim
851	```blade
852	<native:column class="w-full h-full">
853	    {{-- Override only the top bar — the layout's tab bar still renders --}}
854	    <native:top-bar :title="$thread->name" />
855	
856	    <native:scroll-view class="w-full flex-1">
857	        {{-- ... --}}
858	    </native:scroll-view>
859	</native:column>
860	```
861	@endverbatim
862	
863	The same hoisting powers a screen with **no layout at all**: an inline bar alone still produces real native chrome
864	(a `NavigationStack` / `TabView` on iOS, a `Scaffold` / `NavigationBar` on Android), with edge-swipe back, large
865	titles, and Liquid Glass / Material You — identical to what the builders emit. The layout is only worth reaching for
866	when several screens share the same bar. See each element's page for the full attribute surface:
867	[Top Bar](../edge-components/top-bar), [Bottom Navigation](../edge-components/bottom-nav), and
868	[Floating Action Button](../edge-components/fab).
869	
870	<aside>
871	
872	The `custom` attribute is the escape hatch: `<native:top-bar custom>` keeps the bar in the content tree as an
873	ordinary drawn element (for a design a system bar can't express) while *still* suppressing the layout's bar for
874	that slot.
875	
876	</aside>
877
